title: Muon Dynamics as a Spectral Wasserstein Flow
claim: Changing the normalization norm from trace to operator reshapes optimal couplings, producing visibly different matchings between the same source and target distributions.
layout: 4 panels in a row, paired by source-target; matching lines between point clouds
description: A single horizontal strip of four panels labeled (a) p=1, (b) p=∞, (c) p=1, (d) p=∞. Panels (a) and (b) show a blue ring-shaped point cloud on the left and two red disc-shaped clusters on the right. Panels (c) and (d) show a blue rabbit-like silhouette on the left and a red club-suit shape on the right. Thin black line segments connect blue source points to red target points. They show the coupling. Under p=1 the lines are mostly parallel and orderly, with few crossings. Under p=∞ the lines cross and tangle more, with a visibly different pairing. The eye goes first to the dense bundles of black lines between the contrasting blue and red clouds.
caption: Static coupling illustrations for two source-target pairs: exact trace assignments (p = 1) and heuristic operator couplings (p = ∞). Only a subsample of matched segments is displayed.
abstract: Gradient normalization can stabilize deep-learning optimization, and spectral normalizations are especially natural for matrix-shaped parameter blocks; Muon is the motivating example. We study an idealized deterministic, continuous-time, vanishing-momentum version of this idea in the mean-field regime, where wide models are represented by probability measures on parameter space. Starting from normalized matrix flows, we introduce Spectral Wasserstein distances indexed by norms $Î³$ on positive semidefinite matrices: the trace norm recovers the classical $W_2$ distance, the operator norm gives the Muon geometry, and Schatten norms interpolate between them. We develop a static Kantorovich formulation, a max--min robust-cost representation, and Gaussian reductions extending the Bures formula. For monotone norms, we prove equivalence with a Benamou--Brenier formulation and obtain a gradient-flow interpretation of normalized mean-field training dynamics. Numerical experiments illustrate the resulting flows for MMD objectives, Gaussian reductions, two-layer ReLU models, and shallow attention.
